title: Shuffle up from anywhere: remote games and first-hand tests for Brawlternatives
summary: Choose a webcam table, a browser table, or a digital client—and take the right decklist with you.
body:
A new brew deserves a few opening hands before it deserves a shopping cart. Our [Brawlternative shelf](/brawl-box) is built for that curious stage: smaller, theme-first decks that let an idea get onto the table without pretending it is already a polished Commander list. You can test that idea alone, or invite a friend who lives nowhere near your kitchen table. The important part is choosing the right kind of table.

## Choose a remote table that matches the test

### Convoke: keep the paper-table feeling

[Convoke](https://convoke.games/en/) is a webcam Magic platform. Its official site describes friend invites, public tables, card recognition, and in-game card search. This is the natural starting point if you and your friends want to play with physical cards while seeing each other's boards. Set up a camera, agree on the house format, and make sure both players can read the battlefield before starting.

Convoke explicitly documents **Moxfield decklist import**. That is not a promise that this site's Copy button can load a Convoke table directly. Use this handoff instead:

1. Copy or download our generic list.
2. Create or update your deck in Moxfield using its own import controls.
3. Follow Convoke's Moxfield import flow.
4. Review the imported names and quantities rather than assuming the handoff did everything.

### Aura0: a browser table, not an assumed import shortcut

[Aura0](https://aura0.app/) presents an online table with deck selection, drawing, discard and exile zones, an action log, and room-link controls. It offers another way to explore remote tabletop play with friends. The public table is enough to understand the idea; it does not establish a documented direct-import contract for our deck exports.

Open the homepage and inspect the deck controls yourself before planning a session. Use a room you create or are invited to use. We are not publishing a private room link, joining anyone's existing game, or claiming that a deck can be pushed into Aura0 with one click.

### Arena and MTGO: copy once, then import in the client

Our export controls are a one-click **copy or download**, not a one-click installation inside another app. [Arena's official instructions](https://mtgarena-support.wizards.com/hc/en-us/articles/360049857771-Importing-a-Deck) say to copy the list, open **Decks → Import**, and inspect the result. Choose the Arena output so the commander, deck, and any sideboard remain separate. Card availability and the selected format still decide whether the result can actually be played.

[Magic Online's deckbuilding guide](https://www.mtgo.com/getting-started/getting-started-deckbuilding) supports importing text files, pasted lists, and its own .dek files. Our MTGO option provides text; it does not invent the catalog IDs needed for a genuine .dek file. Review zones in the client, especially the commander. MTGO's [official forum discussion](https://forums.mtgo.com/index.php?threads/text-file-commander-decks-import-in-backwards-zones.3196/) explains why commander position in text imports matters.

None of these exports turns a custom 60-card list into an officially supported format. These Brawlternatives are **custom Commander previews, not official Brawl and not regulation 100-card Commander**. Some cards or whole builds may be unavailable or unplayable in either digital client. Agree on a compatible house-rule table instead of treating a successful text import as a legality certificate.

## Run a useful ten-hand test

Before meeting a friend, deal a handful of opening hands with your physical list or your chosen deck tester. For each of ten attempts:

1. Shuffle fully before dealing; do not keep rearranging a bad hand until it looks good.
2. Note the lands and the first meaningful play.
3. Check whether the deck can do its signature thing.
4. Record the result as a quick diagnostic, not proof that a deck is balanced.

For the three finished proposals on the [Brawlternative shelf](/blog/brawlternative-shelf-roundup), watch these deck-specific signals:

- **[The Wise Mothman](/brawl-box/the-wise-mothman):** whether the counter plan develops without running out of cards.
- **[Rakdos, Lord of Riots](/brawl-box/rakdos-lord-of-riots):** whether you can make an opponent lose life **before** trying to cast the commander.
- **[Karlov of the Ghost Council](/brawl-box/karlov-of-the-ghost-council):** separate life-gain events, rather than just the amount of life gained.

Then play real games: interaction changes everything.

## Choose a list and a physical-card path

Ready to pick a list? [Browse the whole Brawlternative shelf](/blog/brawlternative-shelf-roundup), or try one of the [nine Battle Box decks](/blog/battle-box-october-17-recap). On the deck page, use the prominent **Buy Online** action when you want real cards; proxy-print guidance stays optional and secondary. No export button buys cards or spends wildcards for you.

title: Seven Brawlternatives, three finished proposals, and a reason to shuffle each one
summary: The full shelf in one place, with Mothman, Rakdos, and Karlov source lists preserved beside their proposed finishes.
body:
The appeal of this shelf is not that every deck does the same efficient thing. It is that each one asks a different question. Can artifacts turn energy into staying power? Can the graveyard become a second hand? Can a tiny life-gain trigger become a serious threat? These seven builds are invitations to find out.

They share a house label: **Brawlternatives—custom 60-card Commander-preview decks**. They are not official Brawl decks or regulation 100-card Commander decks, and there is no claim that they are tournament-ready or evenly matched. Choose opponents and house rules accordingly. Use the [Brawlternative hub](/brawl-box) to browse the shelf before opening a deck page.

## The three proposed finishes

### [The Wise Mothman](/brawl-box/the-wise-mothman): let the counters tell the story

[The Wise Mothman](/brawl-box/the-wise-mothman) keeps its Fallout-forward radiation, mill, and +1/+1-counter identity. The preserved submission totals 59 cards. The proposed revision corrects three names to **Harold and Bob, First Numens**, **Strong, the Brutish Thespian**, and **Piper Wright, Publick Reporter**. These are name repairs, not three new deck slots.

The actual slot changes are:

- **Out — Abzan Falconer:** outside the commander's Sultai color identity.
- **In — Fathom Mage:** turns counters placed on itself into cards.
- **In — Inspiring Call:** draws for creatures you control with +1/+1 counters and gives those creatures indestructible for the turn.

Together they finish the count at **60**, retain the **22-land** base, and support the deck's existing story rather than replacing it with expensive staples. This is a budget-minded direction, not a live price quote.

### [Rakdos, Lord of Riots](/brawl-box/rakdos-lord-of-riots): the finish is understanding the sequence

[Rakdos, Lord of Riots](/brawl-box/rakdos-lord-of-riots) already has **60 cards and 21 lands**. Its proposed completion keeps every slot, including Leechridden Swamp. The important repair is the sequence:

1. An opponent must already have lost life that turn **before** you cast Rakdos.
2. Once Rakdos is on the battlefield, his reduction affects **later creature spells**.
3. The reduction applies to **generic**, not colored, mana. It does not refund the spell you already cast.

Leechridden Swamp is a setup option, not a free shortcut. It enters tapped; its life-loss activation costs black mana and a tap, and requires two black permanents. Test the early turns honestly before promising spectacular discounted threats. The deck's theatrical payoff is the point, but its mana and sequencing still need to cooperate.

### [Karlov of the Ghost Council](/brawl-box/karlov-of-the-ghost-council): keep both Daxos cards, keep their jobs distinct

[Karlov of the Ghost Council](/brawl-box/karlov-of-the-ghost-council) finishes at **60 cards** with the approved **Crested Sunmare** correction and **Daxos the Returned** replacing Licia. **Daxos, Blessed by the Sun stays**; the two Daxos cards are different cards with different roles. The proposal keeps the source's 20-land base rather than claiming it has been optimized.

Small life-gain events grow Karlov, while the enchantment thread gives Daxos the Returned something to build around. Karlov's exile ability still asks for white-black mana and six counters. A large commander does not gain evasion just because its counters came easily. The splashy finishers are reasons to test the deck, not evidence that it has already passed the test.

Each of these pages separates the proposed list and reasoning from the preserved source history. You can inspect and export the intended version without losing the submitted one. [Scryfall](https://scryfall.com/) card links on the pages supply the rules text behind the changes; representative art is not a statement about which printing anyone owns.

## Four more personalities already on the shelf

- [Dr. Madison Li](/brawl-box/dr-madison-li) brings energy-fueled artifacts, enter-the-battlefield value, and recursion. Start here if you enjoy finding a useful interaction among ordinary-looking pieces.
- [Araumi of the Dead Tide](/brawl-box/araumi-of-the-dead-tide) explores self-mill and encore. Remember that encore depends on the number of opponents; a duel does not produce the same board as a multiplayer pod.
- [Marchesa, the Black Rose](/brawl-box/marchesa-the-black-rose) leans into Grixis treason: borrowed creatures, sacrifice, fiery threats, and recursion. Check whose creatures you control and when the relevant triggers happen rather than treating every theft effect as permanent ownership.
- [Taigam, Sidisi's Hand](/brawl-box/taigam-sidisis-hand) offers blue-black draw-go control, upkeep selection, removal, and graveyard-fueled creature shrinking. It is the patient choice when you would rather hold an answer than race.

Pick a personality, read its plan, and give it a few opening hands. Our [remote-play guide](/blog/remote-play-shuffle-tests) explains which services support a webcam table, a browser table, or a documented text import. On each deck page, **Buy Online** is the main physical-card route: use it when you want to assemble real cards and choose editions, condition, quantities, and shipping yourself. Optional proxy help is secondary. Neither route infers what is missing from anyone's collection.

title: Battle Box notebook: the October 17 recap and nine decks to take to the table
summary: A visual guide to all nine 60-card lists, with today's new deck pages distinguished from the earlier build record.
body:
The [Battle Box hub](/battle-box) is the pick-up-and-play side of this project: nine shared, 60-card decks with different combat rhythms, not nine descriptions of somebody's private collection. This notebook brings the lists together so you can choose a matchup, open a readable deck page, and decide whether to test it online or assemble it in paper.

## Keep the build record straight

This is the requested **October 17 recap**, with a clear distinction between the earlier work and today's additions. The core Battle Box and privacy-first collection tools were already in the October 16 build. The nine dedicated visual deck pages arrived on **October 18**; they should not be backdated as October 17 releases. The available repository record does not establish another Battle Box-specific October 17 release, so this article does not invent one.

The useful result for readers is the connected shelf below. Each deck now has a destination of its own, with the original source order, strategy packages, representative card art, and readable-list view. Those are today's presentation improvements around the existing lists, not a claim that the lists were rebuilt yesterday. The broader official-precon strategy library is a separate feature, not part of these nine 60-card decks.

## Choose the game you want to play

### Fast pressure: start with a short clock

- [Goblin Cavalcade](/battle-box/goblin-cavalcade) turns a crowd of small attackers into pressure.
- [Lightning Burn](/battle-box/lightning-burn) trades flexibility for a much shorter clock.

These are good starting points when you want to find out whether another brew can survive an early challenge.

### Bigger threats: survive the setup turns

- [Kavu Beastmaster](/battle-box/kavu-beastmaster) mixes early exchanges with oversized combat bodies.
- [RG Eldrazi Ramp & Stompy](/battle-box/rg-eldrazi-ramp-stompy) spends early resources on getting to its finishers.

Watch the turns before the big spell, not just how impressive the big spell looks.

### Long games: trade resources carefully

- [Oldschool Zombie Tribal](/battle-box/oldschool-zombie-tribal) makes attrition matter through creatures, recursion, and repeated exchanges.
- [Azorius Control](/battle-box/azorius-control) approaches the same long game from another angle: answers first, a protected finisher later.

Neither name guarantees a balanced matchup against the fastest lists.

### Board development and incremental value

- [Theros Boros Soldiers](/battle-box/theros-boros-soldiers) rewards building a board and targeting the right creature.
- [Simic Evasive Tempo & Midrange](/battle-box/simic-evasive-tempo-midrange) mixes bounce, evasive threats, and incremental value.
- [Mono-White Lifegain & Sunbond Heroic](/battle-box/mono-white-lifegain-sunbond-heroic) connects small life-gain starts with growing threats.

These are distinct play patterns, not a power ranking.

## Buy real cards if that is your preference

**Buy Online** is the primary shopping action on every [deck page](/battle-box). Use it as the physical-card path: the shopping list and retailer search let you choose editions, condition, quantities, and shipping yourself. There is no automatic retailer checkout, no promise of stock or a live deck price, and no purchase is made by following an article link.

Proxy-print help is a smaller, optional route for groups that allow it; see the [proxy-print guide](/battle-box-proxy-print) only if that is the route your group has chosen. Source annotations and rules warnings remain visible; they are not evidence that a visitor owns or lacks any card. Incomplete scans cannot establish a shopping gap.

## Before the first game

Read the deck's source warnings and any house-rule overlay. A deck having 60 cards does not certify normal constructed legality: copy-limit exceptions or other source issues may still need agreement. An optional boss or secret objective is a house rule, not printed card text.

For a remote evening, start with the [service and export guide](/blog/remote-play-shuffle-tests). For a physical session, choose two lists below, assemble them, and write down what actually happened. The next useful improvement should come from games, not from making the recap sound more finished than the evidence allows.

title: Seven commanders that are 100% worth building around
summary: A chapter-by-chapter build-around guide to Sakiko, Meria, Alaundo, Valduk, Memnarch, Denry Klin, and Nikya, with short attributed excerpts from The Commander’s Quarters video.
body:
The Commander’s Quarters video [Commanders That Are 100% Worth Building Around](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Zg1zAsXsQ8) makes a useful distinction: a commander does not need to be the most popular legend in the format to deserve a deck. It needs to create a specific game plan that gives the rest of the list a job. The video’s chapter list moves through seven such commanders: [Sakiko, Mother of Summer](/card/Sakiko%2C%20Mother%20of%20Summer), [Meria, Scholar of Antiquity](/card/Meria%2C%20Scholar%20of%20Antiquity), [Alaundo the Seer](/card/Alaundo%20the%20Seer), [Valduk, Keeper of the Flame](/card/Valduk%2C%20Keeper%20of%20the%20Flame), [Memnarch](/card/Memnarch), [Denry Klin, Editor in Chief](/card/Denry%20Klin%2C%20Editor%20in%20Chief), and [Nikya of the Old Ways](/card/Nikya%20of%20the%20Old%20Ways). The page uses the chapter labels published with the video; it does not imply that every commander is equally strong, equally cheap, or equally easy to pilot.

## How to read the recommendation

The phrase “100% worth building around” is a creative invitation, not a win-rate claim. A build-around commander gives you a constraint that is productive rather than restrictive. It tells you which cards to prioritize, which otherwise powerful cards may be wrong for the list, and what a successful opening hand should be trying to accomplish. That is more useful than treating a commander’s inclusion in a video as a buy signal.

The short excerpts below are transcript-adjacent notes from the analyzed video capture. You can hear the creator’s full wording, context, and sponsor disclosures in the [original YouTube video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Zg1zAsXsQ8). They are intentionally kept short and labeled as capture excerpts rather than presented as a certified verbatim transcript.

> “100% worth building around.” — on-screen title and central thesis of the video. [1]

> “Massive mana engine based on combat damage.” — capture excerpt describing the Sakiko thesis. [1]

> “Insane amounts of mana.” — capture excerpt from the Sakiko discussion. [1]

## Sakiko, Mother of Summer: turn combat into a mana reserve

Sakiko is the clearest example of a commander that tells you what the deck is supposed to do. Her combat-damage trigger turns damage dealt to players into green mana, and that mana does not disappear merely because a step or phase ends. The resulting list should not be a generic Gruul creature pile. It should be built to connect with players, preserve access to the mana, and convert one successful combat into a sequence of oversized plays.

The important deckbuilding question is not simply “which green creatures are strongest?” It is “which creatures make combat damage reliable?” Evasion, trample, haste, protection, and effects that widen the attack all have a direct relationship to Sakiko’s engine. The payoff package can then include large hydras, expensive threats, and spells that are normally awkward because the deck has created an unusually large mana turn. If the list spends all of its slots on expensive cards but cannot connect, it has copied the payoff without building the engine.

Start testing with a simple loop: establish one attacker that is hard to block, attack a player, count the mana Sakiko created, and ask whether the next spell converts that mana into more pressure or more cards. That test is more revealing than a goldfish that assumes every creature survives. Sakiko is worth building because the commander changes the value of combat itself.

## Meria, Scholar of Antiquity: artifacts that are also resources

Meria asks for a different kind of discipline. The commander rewards a deck that treats noncreature artifacts as useful permanents rather than as isolated equipment or incidental mana rocks. The best version of the idea gives those artifacts multiple jobs: they can help develop mana, provide cards or selection, become attackers when needed, and remain relevant after the first exchange.

A Meria list should therefore separate its artifacts into roles. Cheap artifacts help Meria start producing value early. Utility artifacts keep the deck from stalling when the table removes the commander. Payoffs reward the deck for tapping or sacrificing artifacts, while creature-artifact support helps the deck keep applying pressure instead of turning into a pile of inert permanents. The central question is whether each artifact advances the plan when Meria is on the battlefield and remains acceptable when she is not.

The video’s inclusion of Meria is a good reminder that a commander can be worth building even when its theme is familiar. “Artifacts” is not a complete strategy by itself. Meria gives the theme a particular rhythm: deploy inexpensive objects, turn them into access to more resources, and use the resulting velocity to make the board difficult to exhaust.

## Alaundo the Seer: time, cards, and delayed pressure

Alaundo rewards a player who is comfortable making the present turn serve a later turn. The commander’s design points toward a list that can put cards into motion, use counters or delayed timing as part of its plan, and eventually turn those investments into a large burst of activity. That means the deck needs more than expensive spells. It needs a way to survive while its delayed resources mature.

The best Alaundo builds make the waiting period productive. Card selection helps choose what should be committed. Protection keeps the commander or the critical permanent on the table. Untap effects and cost discipline can increase the number of meaningful activations without forcing every game to follow the same scripted line. A good list also includes ordinary interaction, because a delayed plan still has to answer an opponent who is winning now.

Build Alaundo if you enjoy seeing a plan develop across several turns. The reward is not merely a large spell. It is the feeling that an earlier decision has become a second wave of action at exactly the moment the table thought your resources were spent.

## Valduk, Keeper of the Flame: make temporary equipment count

Valduk is a focused combat commander. The deck’s question is how to turn a collection of Auras and Equipment into immediate pressure without running out of material after a single attack. The temporary Elemental bodies created by Valduk mean that the list cares about the quantity and quality of attachments, but it also has to care about timing. A card that looks efficient on an empty battlefield may be poor if it does not help Valduk attack or if it strands the deck after a board wipe.

A useful Valduk shell mixes cheap attachments, cards that replace themselves, and ways to make one large attack matter. Haste and evasion raise the floor of the token plan. Recursion and protection raise the ceiling by allowing the deck to rebuild. The commander is worth building because the deck’s cards are connected by a visible rule: attachments are not just enhancements; they are the material that creates the attack.

This is also a good commander for a clear budget build. Expensive staples can improve the ceiling, but the strategy remains legible when the list starts with common and uncommon Auras, inexpensive Equipment, and a careful curve. The build should be judged by whether it can make a meaningful attack repeatedly, not by whether one turn produces the largest possible token count.

## Memnarch: a long-game artifact-control project

Memnarch is the most openly ambitious commander in the group. The attraction is not subtle: artifacts become permanents you can interact with, and the deck can eventually make the table’s resources feel provisional. That kind of control plan needs a serious mana base and a realistic understanding of how much attention the commander will attract. The deck cannot assume that Memnarch will survive indefinitely once opponents understand what the activations represent.

The responsible build therefore protects its mana engine without becoming all engine. Cheap artifacts and rocks establish the ability to activate Memnarch. Card draw finds both protection and action. Flexible interaction buys the turns needed to accumulate resources. The list should also have a plan for games in which the commander is removed repeatedly, because a strategy that only works with Memnarch on the battlefield is not a strategy; it is a single permanent waiting to be answered.

Memnarch is worth building for the player who enjoys a slow, expressive artifact-control game and accepts the social cost of a commander that can dominate a developed board. It is not an automatic recommendation for every table. Ask first whether your playgroup enjoys that kind of escalating control, then build the deck to make its threat level visible rather than surprising.

## Denry Klin, Editor in Chief: counters with a board-development engine

Denry Klin rewards a deck that can place counters on creatures and then preserve the value of those counters as the board changes. The commander turns a familiar +1/+1-counter theme into a question about distribution and timing. Which creature should receive the first investment? Which creature should carry a counter when Denry leaves? Which cards turn a counter into cards, mana, evasion, or protection instead of merely making a body larger?

A strong Denry list should include redundant counter enablers and payoffs that work at different points on the curve. Early creatures give the deck something to develop. Midgame engines convert counters into cards or additional board presence. Finishers make the accumulated counters matter in combat. The list should avoid making every payoff dependent on one perfect sequence; the commander is most interesting when several modest permanents can combine into a board that keeps improving.

Denry is a good “build it your way” commander. You can lean toward tokens, modular artifacts, proliferate, or a more conventional creature deck, but each direction should answer the same question: how does this card make the counter plan more consistent? If the answer is only “it is a large creature,” the build is missing the reason the commander was selected.

## Nikya of the Old Ways: accept the creature-only constraint

Nikya is a commander that rewards commitment. The creature-only restriction changes what the deck can use for interaction, ramp, and card advantage, while the mana ability compensates by making creature-heavy development much more explosive. The build should not hide from that constraint by filling the list with cards that do not belong to its central plan. It should find creatures that perform the jobs normally assigned to noncreature spells.

Creature-based removal, artifact and enchantment answers, fight effects, land-search creatures, and creature-based card advantage all become more important. The list can then use the extra mana to deploy a board that makes the restriction feel like an advantage rather than a punishment. The tension is real: a creature-only deck can be powerful and consistent, but it must respect the kinds of permanents it cannot answer efficiently.

Nikya is worth building when you enjoy solving deckbuilding problems. The fun is not just casting large creatures. It is discovering which creatures can serve as ramp, removal, recursion, protection, or card flow while still contributing to the battlefield. That is a genuine build-around constraint, and it gives the finished deck a personality that a generic Gruul ramp list may not have.

## What I would build first

For a first project, Sakiko and Meria offer the clearest feedback loops. Sakiko tells you immediately whether your creatures can connect and whether your payoffs use the mana well. Meria tells you whether your artifacts are doing enough work to justify their slots. Valduk is the most approachable combat project, while Denry Klin is a flexible choice for a player who wants to tune the list around a preferred counter package.

Alaundo, Memnarch, and Nikya ask for more patience. Alaundo needs careful sequencing. Memnarch needs a table conversation as well as a mana engine. Nikya needs the discipline to replace familiar noncreature answers with creatures that perform comparable jobs. Those are not reasons to skip them. They are reasons to choose them deliberately.

The practical next step is to open the [Commander Library](/commander), choose one of the seven card profiles above, and write down the deck’s first three jobs before buying anything. Then use the video’s [card-list link and original discussion](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9Zg1zAsXsQ8) as a second opinion. The video supplies the spark; your games should decide which version deserves a permanent place in your library.

## Source and attribution notes

This feature is an editorial reading of The Commander’s Quarters video, not a reproduction of its decklist. The public YouTube page identifies Mitch’s channel, the October 25, 2026 publication date, and chapters for the seven commanders named above. The video also includes creator plugs and sponsorship material; those are part of the original viewing context, not endorsements by this site. Prices, availability, and “worth building” judgments are not treated as verified investment advice. Card rules text and current printing data should be checked on the linked card profiles before purchasing or finalizing a list.
dataWindow: YouTube video published October 25, 2026; chapters and public metadata checked October 25, 2026.
caveat: The source page identifies the seven chaptered commanders, but the available automated capture did not provide a complete verbatim transcript. Short excerpts are labeled as transcript-adjacent capture notes; use the linked video for exact wording and full context.

title: Simple builds, serious pressure: eight commanders that can dominate a playgroup
summary: A commander-by-commander showcase of the simple build plans in The Commander’s Quarters video, from Jasmine’s vanilla evasion to Ruric Thar’s spell punishment.
body:
The Commander’s Quarters video [Commanders With Super Simple Builds That Will DOMINATE Your Playgroup!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8KK0-U8FAc) is built around a useful Commander lesson: a deck can be straightforward without being shallow. Mitch’s examples each reduce the build to a small number of visible jobs—play hard-to-block creatures, reach 21 commander damage, turn toughness into power, cast spells for tokens, bank mana, or double a creature and throw it at someone.

This companion feature showcases every commander discussed in the public chapter sequence and the later transcript segment: [Jasmine Boreal of the Seven](/card/Jasmine%20Boreal%20of%20the%20Seven), [Yargle and Multani](/card/Yargle%20and%20Multani), [Arcades, the Strategist](/card/Arcades%2C%20the%20Strategist), [Edric, Spymaster of Trest](/card/Edric%2C%20Spymaster%20of%20Trest), [Ovika, Enigma Goliath](/card/Ovika%2C%20Enigma%20Goliath), [Omnath, Locus of Mana](/card/Omnath%2C%20Locus%20of%20Mana), [Mr. Orfeo, the Boulder](/card/Mr.%20Orfeo%2C%20the%20Boulder), and [Ruric Thar, the Unbowed](/card/Ruric%20Thar%2C%20the%20Unbowed). The YouTube page’s visible chapter panel lists the first seven; the retrieved public captions continue into the Ruric Thar discussion, so it is included and labeled accordingly.

## The simple-build test

A simple build should pass three tests. First, you should be able to explain the deck’s plan in one sentence without naming twenty cards. Second, the commander should make ordinary cards better by giving them a shared purpose. Third, the plan should still leave room for interaction and recovery. “Simple” does not mean “skip protection,” “ignore the mana curve,” or “assume nobody has a board wipe.” It means the deck’s decisions remain legible when you draw an opening hand.

The excerpts below are short, time-stamped quotes from the public captions. They preserve Mitch’s conversational delivery and are linked to the original video for full context. They are source excerpts, not an endorsement of a guaranteed win rate.

> “Commanders that have super simple builds that will absolutely dominate your play group.” — 0:17–0:25

> “Your creatures are near unblockable.” — 0:52–1:01, on Jasmine’s vanilla-creature plan

> “Hey, can you count to 21?” — 4:55–5:05, on Yargle and Multani

> “Get a bunch of evasive low-to-the-ground creatures out, swing, draw an insane amount of cards.” — 8:41–8:54, on Edric

> “Non-creature spell focus. Great. Okay, do that.” — 14:34–14:45, on Ovika’s shell

## Jasmine Boreal of the Seven: vanilla creatures become evasive threats

Jasmine is the most literal expression of the video’s “simple build” idea. The deck wants creatures without abilities, then uses Jasmine’s rules text to make those creatures difficult for ability-bearing creatures to block. That constraint is productive: instead of searching for creatures with the longest text boxes, you search for efficient bodies that hit hard and leave the commander’s evasion clause intact.

The transcript highlights Quake Strider Ceratops as a large payoff and Borborygmos as an anthem that does not add abilities to the creatures being enhanced. Unnatural Growth gives the board another dramatic power increase. The warning is just as important as the payoff: do not casually add trample or other abilities to the creatures if doing so removes the evasion condition you built the deck to exploit.

**Showcase plan:** mana acceleration, large vanilla creatures, ability-free anthems, and protection. Jasmine is a good choice when you want a deck whose card-selection rule is visible before the first game begins.

## Yargle and Multani: count to 21

Yargle and Multani begins close to the Commander-damage threshold with an enormous printed power. The list does not need a complicated combo to create pressure; it needs ways to make that power connect. Mitch points to Indomitable Might as a way to increase power and let the enchanted creature assign combat damage as though it were not blocked, Rogue’s Passage as repeatable evasion, and Tyvar’s Stand as both protection and a pump spell.

The simple line is easy to test: cast the commander, find a way to make an attack connect, and count the damage. That does not make the deck automatic. Removal, timing, and commander-tax pressure still matter. But the build has a clean feedback loop: every protection spell can also help finish the game, and every evasion effect turns a very large creature into a genuine clock.

**Showcase plan:** pump, evasion, protection, and a few ways to use the commander’s large power twice—once in combat and, if necessary, again as a resource.

## Arcades, the Strategist: walls that draw cards and attack

Arcades turns defenders from defensive infrastructure into a card-drawing, attacking board. The deck’s search instruction is simple: prioritize creatures with defender, low mana costs, and high toughness. When those creatures enter, Arcades supplies cards; when they attack, their toughness becomes their damage output.

The transcript calls out Wall of Denial as an efficient high-toughness body with flying and shroud. It also describes defender-based mana creatures and Tower Defense as a card that changes from a defensive trick into a large team-wide pump. Blink effects add another layer by reusing defender enter-the-battlefield triggers and protecting a developed board.

**Showcase plan:** cheap high-toughness defenders, defender-based ramp, toughness payoffs, card draw, and blink or protection. Arcades is ideal for players who like a board that looks harmless until its defensive numbers suddenly become lethal.

## Edric, Spymaster of Trest: evasive creatures become cards

Edric’s deck is a low-to-the-ground tempo engine. The list starts with one-mana or two-mana creatures that are difficult to block, then uses combat damage to generate cards. Slither Blade represents the basic plan: establish a cheap evasive attacker early, deploy Edric, and turn successful attacks into a stream of options. Siren Stormtamer adds utility because it can protect a commander or important creature by countering a spell or ability that targets it.

Scale Up illustrates the deck’s finishing package. Small evasive creatures remain evasive after becoming much larger, so the deck can turn a board of modest attackers into a lethal swing without abandoning the original plan. The danger is overextending into a wipe, which is why the deck should treat card flow as a way to hold up protection, not merely as permission to empty its hand.

**Showcase plan:** cheap evasive creatures, combat-damage card draw, protective utility creatures, and a small number of efficient pump effects.

## Ovika, Enigma Goliath: cast noncreature spells, make hasty Goblins

Ovika’s build can be summarized as “turn the noncreature spells you already want to cast into an army.” The commander creates hasty Phyrexian Goblins based on the mana value of each noncreature spell. That means ramp, card draw, and payoffs all need to be chosen with a second question in mind: how many bodies does this spell create, and what do those bodies do after they arrive?

The transcript emphasizes mana rocks, card advantage, and team-wide pump. Harmonize Crescendo is presented as a way to draw from a growing Phyrexian board, while Shared Animosity turns a wide Goblin or Phyrexian attack into a scaling threat. The deck is simple because its categories are clear, but it still needs a curve that lets Ovika arrive before the hand is empty.

**Showcase plan:** accelerate into Ovika, cast profitable noncreature spells, refill with tribal or creature-count draw, and convert the hasty token mass into combat damage.

## Omnath, Locus of Mana: save green mana and turn it into power

Omnath is a mana bank with a body attached. Unspent green mana remains available and increases Omnath’s power, so the deck can spend one turn developing resources and another turn converting that stored mana into a large creature, a protected attack, or both. The simplicity comes from respecting the commander’s central instruction: produce green mana, keep it, and decide when it is worth spending.

Wilderness Reclamation creates another opportunity to tap lands and rebuild the mana pool. Mana Reflection multiplies the output of the deck’s mana permanents. Whispersilk Cloak turns the stored mana into a credible Voltron finish by providing protection and evasion. The deck should still include interaction, because saving mana is only useful if the player can preserve the board or choose a safe moment to attack.

**Showcase plan:** land-based ramp, mana multipliers, ways to use excess mana, and a protected commander-damage finish.

## Mr. Orfeo, the Boulder: double power, then convert it into damage

Mr. Orfeo’s text is compact: when you attack, double a target creature’s power. The deck therefore has two jobs. It needs creatures with unusually high power for their cost, and it needs multiple ways to turn that power into damage. Mitch describes his version as “Hotline Fling,” using sacrifice-to-damage effects to make a creature that attacked one opponent matter to a second opponent as well.

Grakmaw, Arisen Titan supplies a large body, while Wilderness Elemental can scale from opponents’ nonbasic lands and become enormous when its power is doubled. Fling is the obvious payoff: attack, double the creature, then sacrifice it to send that power at another target. The plan is explosive but not invisible, so the deck benefits from choosing the right attack and holding enough protection to avoid losing the entire turn to a removal spell.

**Showcase plan:** oversized creatures, power doublers, attack triggers, and sacrifice outlets that turn combat power into direct damage.

## Ruric Thar, the Unbowed: punish the spells your opponents want to cast

Ruric Thar is the video’s cleanest punishment engine. The commander attacks when able and deals six damage to a player who casts a noncreature spell. The build therefore leans into creatures: the deck wants to deploy threats and creature-based support while making the table think twice before using ordinary removal, tutors, sweepers, or card-draw spells.

The important limitation is social and strategic. Ruric Thar does not stop noncreature spells; it taxes them with damage. Opponents can still decide that six life is worth paying, and the deck still needs answers to permanents that slip through. Somberwald Sage and Nikya of the Old Ways illustrate the creature-based acceleration direction discussed in this portion of the transcript. Build enough creature interaction that the restriction feels like a plan rather than a self-imposed gap.

**Showcase plan:** creature-heavy ramp, creature-based answers, large attackers, and a clear conversation with the playgroup about how much punishment the table wants in its games.

## Which simple build should you choose?

Choose Jasmine if you enjoy deckbuilding constraints and combat that rewards clean vanilla bodies. Choose Yargle and Multani if you want the most direct commander-damage challenge. Arcades is the pick for a wall engine with card draw; Edric is the pick for cheap evasive creatures and a fast hand. Ovika turns ordinary mana rocks and draw spells into bodies. Omnath rewards patient resource management. Mr. Orfeo turns a single attack into a multi-angle finisher. Ruric Thar is for the player who wants creatures to be the answer to a spell-heavy table.

The useful next step is not to buy every card named in the video. Open the [Commander Library](/commander), choose one showcase, and write three rules for the first draft: what the deck must do early, what it does when the commander is removed, and how it closes a game. Then watch the [full Commander’s Quarters video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8KK0-U8FAc), review its [card list](https://partner.tcgplayer.com/tcq_simple-dominant-cmdr), and test the list against the actual playgroup you intend to face.

## Source notes and affiliate disclosure

This feature is based on the public YouTube video, its public captions, and the public chapter metadata checked October 25, 2026. The video’s description links to TCGplayer decklists and says those links are affiliate links. This site does not reproduce the full decklists, guarantee prices, or treat the creator’s “dominate” framing as a verified win-rate claim. Card names and rules interactions should be checked against current Oracle text before a purchase or deck export.
dataWindow: YouTube video published May 31, 2026; public captions, chapters, and source links checked October 25, 2026.
caveat: The public chapter panel lists the first seven showcases; the retrieved captions continue into a Ruric Thar segment, which is included and explicitly labeled in the article. The separate ten-commander MTG Daily Drop page is a different source and was not merged into this feature.

title: Eight simple Commander deck blueprints: from vanilla evasion to spell punishment
summary: Turn the Commander’s Quarters simple-build ideas into practical deck shells with opening-hand tests, win plans, and honest failure modes.
body:
The first feature covered the eight commanders in The Commander’s Quarters video [Commanders With Super Simple Builds That Will DOMINATE Your Playgroup!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8KK0-U8FAc). This follow-up turns those ideas into practical deck blueprints.

These are not claimed-to-be-final 100-card lists. They are **construction briefs**: each one gives you a commander, a small number of deck packages, an opening-hand test, a way to close the game, and a warning about the plan’s most obvious failure mode. Use the briefs to start a list in the [Commander Library](/commander), then tune the exact cards for your budget, collection, and playgroup.

## How to turn a video idea into a deck

A commander’s theme is only the beginning. A functional list needs a mana plan, a way to keep seeing cards, interaction, protection, and a closing package. For these eight builds, start with the commander’s central verb: **sneak**, **connect**, **defend**, **draw**, **cast**, **save**, **double**, or **punish**.

For a first draft, give every card a job label. If a card does not help the central verb, produce mana, draw cards, protect the plan, or answer a serious problem, it needs a strong reason to stay. This keeps a simple build from turning into a pile of cards that merely share a color identity.

## Jasmine Boreal: vanilla evasion midrange

**The shell:** [Jasmine Boreal of the Seven](/card/Jasmine%20Boreal%20of%20the%20Seven), efficient creatures with no abilities, creature ramp, ability-free anthems, and protection. The key constraint is not just “play big creatures.” It is “play creatures whose lack of abilities preserves Jasmine’s evasion condition.”

**Opening-hand test:** keep a hand that can produce mana, deploy an early body or ramp piece, and reach a meaningful creature before the table has established a wall of tokens. A hand full of expensive vanilla creatures with no acceleration is a mulligan even if the top end looks impressive.

**Game plan:** develop mana, establish a board of clean bodies, and use effects such as large pumps or anthems that do not add unwanted abilities. Make attacks when the defending creatures are least able to block. Protection matters because rebuilding a board of large creatures is slower than rebuilding a board of one-drops.

**Close:** a wide attack backed by a power-doubling effect or a large single threat. Treat trample and other added abilities carefully; a flashy upgrade can interfere with the reason the deck works.

**Main weakness:** token-heavy tables can produce enough ability-free blockers to make the evasion clause less reliable. Build some answers to go-wide boards rather than assuming every opponent’s creatures have relevant abilities.

### Budget upgrade guide

Start with inexpensive mana creatures and efficient vanilla bodies before chasing premium finishers. Replace tapped dual lands with basics and budget duals until the deck’s curve is stable. The highest-impact low-cost upgrades are usually protection, repeatable card draw, and a few cheap board-wide pumps that do not add abilities to your creatures. Spend next on cards that make the first attack safer; a modest creature that connects is worth more than a flashy six-mana threat stranded in hand.

## Yargle and Multani: commander-damage Voltron

**The shell:** [Yargle and Multani](/card/Yargle%20and%20Multani), pump effects, evasion, protection, and a few cards that let the commander’s power matter outside ordinary combat. This is the cleanest blueprint in the group: get to 21 commander damage as efficiently as possible.

**Opening-hand test:** look for enough lands to cast the commander, one way to protect or increase it, and one way to make the attack connect. A hand with only pump and no evasion is incomplete; a hand with only evasion and no way to survive a removal spell is equally fragile.

**Game plan:** cast the commander at the right moment, not merely as soon as possible. Use protection that can also act as a pump spell when available. Keep track of commander tax, because the deck’s entire clock depends on being able to recast the threat without spending the whole game recovering.

**Close:** one clean hit, a second attack after a protection spell, or a damage-through-blockers effect that turns Yargle’s printed power into lethal commander damage. The plan should be obvious to opponents, so sequencing and patience are part of the deck’s power.

**Main weakness:** a single exile effect or repeated chump blockers can buy the table enough time. Include card draw and redundant evasion rather than treating the commander as the only card that matters.

### Budget upgrade guide

Build the connection package first. Low-cost effects that grant evasion, protection, or pseudo-unblockability will improve the deck more than expensive equipment that only increases power. Use flexible pump spells that can protect Yargle as well as increase damage, and favor lands or creatures that provide evasion without consuming a full spell slot. Upgrade the mana base last; this deck benefits more from reliably casting and protecting its commander than from premium lands that do not advance the kill.

## Arcades: defender tempo and toughness

**The shell:** [Arcades, the Strategist](/card/Arcades%2C%20the%20Strategist), cheap defenders with high toughness, defender-based mana, enter-the-battlefield draw, toughness pumps, and blink or protection. The deck should be able to function as a defensive wall deck before Arcades arrives and become an attacking engine after it resolves.

**Opening-hand test:** keep hands that have early defenders and either Arcades, a way to find the commander, or enough draw to keep developing. A hand with only expensive walls is not a plan. Your first creatures should either protect you, produce mana, or replace themselves.

**Game plan:** deploy low-cost walls, draw when they enter, and make your toughness total matter in combat. Blink effects can reuse your best triggers, while a toughness pump can turn a board that looked defensive into a lethal attack. Hold some protection for Arcades because the draw engine and combat conversion both disappear when the commander is gone.

**Close:** a wide wall attack after a toughness boost, a blink sequence that rebuilds the hand, or a single high-toughness creature that becomes a serious evasive threat. Arcades rewards a board that looks underpowered until the combat math changes.

**Main weakness:** creature sweepers reset both your board and your card engine. Include recovery, a few noncreature ways to draw or protect, and enough lands to rebuild instead of relying entirely on a single commander cast.

### Budget upgrade guide

The budget version should begin with the cheapest high-toughness defenders that draw a card, produce mana, or protect the table. Prioritize redundancy over individually famous walls. A few inexpensive blink effects and toughness pumps can do more work than costly staples because they reuse the engine and create surprise damage. Once the shell is consistent, upgrade the lands and add premium protection; Arcades already supplies much of the deck’s card advantage.

## Edric: evasive tempo and combat-damage cards

**The shell:** [Edric, Spymaster of Trest](/card/Edric%2C%20Spymaster%20of%20Trest), one- and two-mana evasive creatures, cheap protection, combat tricks, and a small number of finishers. The list wants to turn every successful attack into another decision rather than waiting for one enormous battlefield.

**Opening-hand test:** prioritize two or three early creatures, lands, and a plan to cast Edric while those creatures can still connect. A hand with only late-game evasive creatures misses the deck’s advantage. A hand with creatures but no second land should not be kept merely because Edric is powerful.

**Game plan:** encourage attacks that produce cards, use politics carefully, and keep enough mana available to protect the commander or an important attacker. Small utility creatures can do double duty as evasive threats and defensive answers. Do not spend every card-draw turn emptying your hand into a board wipe.

**Close:** a wide evasive attack supported by a pump spell, an extra-turn effect that fits your group’s expectations, or a protected board that keeps generating more cards than opponents can answer. Edric is strongest when the table is forced to respect several small attackers at once.

**Main weakness:** creature sweepers and pillow-fort effects can interrupt the combat engine. Include bounce or other flexible interaction and a few ways to win when creatures cannot connect immediately.

### Budget upgrade guide

This deck wants quantity and reliability, not expensive threats. Fill the first draft with inexpensive creatures that cannot be blocked, have flying, or carry useful protection text. Budget counterspells, bounce, and combat tricks can protect the draw engine while keeping mana open. Spend upgrades on the mana curve and card selection before premium extra-turn effects; if the deck connects early and keeps drawing, it can close games without a luxury finisher.

## Ovika: noncreature spells into hasty Phyrexians

**The shell:** [Ovika, Enigma Goliath](/card/Ovika%2C%20Enigma%20Goliath), mana rocks, noncreature ramp and draw, token payoffs, tribal card advantage, and a few finishers. Every noncreature spell should be evaluated twice: what does it do on the stack, and how many hasty bodies does it create after Ovika resolves?

**Opening-hand test:** keep mana, acceleration, and at least one profitable noncreature spell. Ovika costs enough that a hand full of token payoffs without ramp is too slow. The best early hands are not necessarily explosive; they are the ones that can reach Ovika with cards still in hand.

**Game plan:** accelerate, cast Ovika, and chain spells that produce value while building a wide board. Draw effects scale with the growing Phyrexian presence. Mana rocks continue to matter because they both accelerate future spells and increase token production when those spells resolve.

**Close:** a wide hasty swing, a tribal draw spell that refills into another turn of action, or a pump effect that turns a group of small tokens into lethal damage. Sequence the first post-Ovika spells so the deck still has mana for protection or a second wave.

**Main weakness:** Ovika is expensive and attracts removal before the engine begins. Use a mix of haste-independent value, recursion, and enough card draw to rebuild. Do not fill the deck with expensive noncreature spells that look powerful but leave you unable to cast anything after the commander is answered.

### Budget upgrade guide

Begin with affordable mana rocks, cantrips, rummage effects, and token payoffs that each create value before and after Ovika enters. The best budget upgrades are spells that draw a card, make multiple bodies, or serve as interaction while still triggering the commander. Avoid filling the list with expensive haymakers that leave you empty-handed after one removal spell. Upgrade the draw engine and protection package before premium tribal finishers.

## Omnath: the mana-bank Voltron deck

**The shell:** [Omnath, Locus of Mana](/card/Omnath%2C%20Locus%20of%20Mana), land ramp, mana multipliers, ways to spend excess mana, protection, and evasion. The deck’s resource is not just lands; it is the green mana you deliberately leave unspent.

**Opening-hand test:** keep lands and a ramp path that lets you increase the mana pool without emptying it immediately. A hand with a large finisher but no way to generate surplus green mana is not an Omnath hand. A protection spell is especially valuable because it preserves both the commander and the mana investment represented by its power.

**Game plan:** develop lands, bank mana, and choose between deploying a threat, holding up interaction, or growing Omnath. Untap effects and mana multipliers compound the plan, but the deck should not become so focused on producing mana that it forgets to use it. Treat the mana pool as a flexible reserve rather than a number you must maximize every turn.

**Close:** protect Omnath, grant evasion, and deliver commander damage, or convert the stored mana into a board that can survive if Omnath is removed. A good list can win through the commander without requiring every game to be a one-shot attack.

**Main weakness:** removal resets the threat while the mana itself disappears between turns unless the commander’s ability preserves it. Include alternate mana sinks, card draw, and a recovery plan for a commander-taxed Omnath.

### Budget upgrade guide

Prioritize basic-land ramp, landfall-style untap effects, and inexpensive ways to spend excess mana. Protection and evasion are the most important budget purchases because they convert the mana bank into an actual win. Mana multipliers can wait until the deck reliably produces surplus green mana; a cheap ramp spell that advances the next two turns is better than a costly multiplier that sits dead early. Improve the land count and curve before upgrading individual finishers.

## Mr. Orfeo: power doubling and fling damage

**The shell:** [Mr. Orfeo, the Boulder](/card/Mr.%20Orfeo%2C%20the%20Boulder), oversized creatures, creatures with attack triggers, power doublers, sacrifice outlets, and direct-damage effects. The deck has two targets: the opponent in combat and the opponent who thinks combat is over.

**Opening-hand test:** find lands, one early creature or ramp piece, and either a large body or a way to locate one. The deck should not keep a hand that relies on drawing both Orfeo and a finisher without a backup plan. A sacrifice outlet can be as important as a combat trick because it lets one attack matter twice.

**Game plan:** develop a creature whose power is worth doubling, attack when Orfeo’s trigger is safe, and preserve the option to convert that power into direct damage. Do not expose every large creature before you can protect or exploit it. A modest creature with a reliable sacrifice line can be better than a larger creature that only attacks.

**Close:** double a large attacker, connect in combat, and then sacrifice it to finish or pressure another opponent. Alternatively, use a power-doubling combat to eliminate one player while keeping the sacrifice line available for a second target.

**Main weakness:** creature removal breaks the conversion chain, and the deck can lose a full turn if a large creature is answered before the attack. Use haste, protection, recursion, and several kinds of payoff so the deck does not depend on one “perfect” Fling turn.

### Budget upgrade guide

The budget shell can use oversized creatures with drawbacks, creatures that scale from the board state, and inexpensive sacrifice outlets. Prioritize redundant ways to convert power into damage so one removal spell does not erase the entire plan. Combat tricks that protect a creature or double as removal are excellent early upgrades. Save premium tutors and expensive doublers for later; the deck’s biggest gain usually comes from better sequencing and more reliable sacrifice outlets.

## Ruric Thar: creature-heavy punishment

**The shell:** [Ruric Thar, the Unbowed](/card/Ruric%20Thar%2C%20the%20Unbowed), creature-based ramp, creature-based removal and interaction, large attackers, and a small number of noncreature spells reserved for effects the deck cannot reasonably replace. The point is not to prevent opponents from casting spells; it is to make each choice expensive while your own deck keeps developing with creatures.

**Opening-hand test:** keep lands, creature ramp, and an early board presence. A hand full of ordinary instants and sorceries is fighting the commander’s identity. You need enough action before Ruric Thar so the table cannot simply wait while you spend six mana on a threat.

**Game plan:** establish a creature advantage, cast Ruric Thar when opponents are likely to need noncreature spells, and use creature-based answers to keep pressure on the board. The deck should communicate its plan clearly with the playgroup. Punishment effects are more fun when the table knows what sort of game it is agreeing to play.

**Close:** attack with a large creature board while opponents choose between taking six damage and leaving a problem unanswered. Creature-based pump, combat tricks, and haste can shorten the game before the table assembles a clean answer.

**Main weakness:** Ruric Thar does not stop removal, and some decks are happy to pay six life for a decisive spell. Include enough creature interaction and resilient threats that your plan remains functional when opponents ignore the tax.

### Budget upgrade guide

Use creatures as the budget replacements for ramp, removal, and card advantage. Land-search creatures, fight creatures, artifact or enchantment removal on bodies, and creature-based draw keep the restriction meaningful without requiring expensive staples. Prioritize haste, resilient threats, and answers to problematic permanents before adding luxury lock pieces. A consistent creature curve makes Ruric Thar threatening; a pricey collection of top-end creatures does not help if the deck cannot develop before turn six.

## Build one, then compare the games

These eight blueprints are deliberately different. Jasmine and Arcades ask you to respect a deckbuilding constraint. Yargle and Omnath ask you to protect one large resource. Edric asks you to turn small attacks into velocity. Ovika asks you to make normal spells do double duty. Mr. Orfeo asks you to convert combat into direct damage. Ruric Thar asks you to build around the kind of spells your table wants to cast.

Start with one commander, not all eight. Play ten opening hands and record the first meaningful play, the turn the commander arrived, the first turn you felt threatened, and what actually ended the game. That information is more useful than a goldfish turn that assumes no one interacts. If the deck repeatedly fails at the same job, change the package that supports that job instead of adding more unrelated power.

When you are ready, browse the [Commander Library](/commander), review the [simple-build feature](/blog/simple-builds-that-dominate-your-playgroup), and use the [original Commander’s Quarters video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x8KK0-U8FAc) as the source discussion. The video supplies the premise; the games decide which blueprint earns a permanent slot.

## Source and decklist note

This is an editorial deck-construction companion to The Commander’s Quarters video. It does not reproduce the creator’s full decklists, certify Commander legality for every proposed card, or promise a win rate. Card rules text, prices, editions, and availability should be checked independently before purchase or export. “Dominate” is the video’s framing, not a verified investment or competitive-performance claim.
dataWindow: Editorial deckbuilding companion published October 28, 2026; source video and public captions checked October 25, 2026.
caveat: These are construction briefs, not complete decklists or guaranteed win-rate claims. Verify current Oracle text, legality, prices, and availability before building or buying.

title: Invisible Woman: Build the Wall, Then Break the Table
summary: A collection-aware upgrade path for turning The Fantastic Four precon into defensive spellslinger tokens with Walls, card advantage, and a budget-conscious route to lethal combat.
body:
# Invisible Woman: Build the Wall, Then Break the Table

The Fantastic Four precon is at its best when it feels like a team rather than a pile of four-color staples. With **Invisible Woman, Sue Storm** in the command zone, the deck has a clear identity: cast a noncreature spell, create the defensive infrastructure to survive, then turn that board into a safe and surprisingly wide attack.

The stock list already has a strong base. **Sol Ring, Arcane Signet, Farseek, Cultivate, Three Visits,** and **Chromatic Lantern** handle much of the fixing. **Invisible Force Field, Clever Concealment,** and the Wall-producing commander give the deck a defensive posture, while the Fantastic Four themselves provide alternate ways to build the deck later. The upgrade should not erase that identity. It should make Invisible Woman’s trigger happen more often and make every trigger matter more.

## The finding: this is defensive spellslinger tokens

Invisible Woman is not simply a four-color good-stuff commander, and she is not only a Wall commander. Her most reliable version sits at the intersection of three plans:

- **Spell velocity:** cast a cheap instant, sorcery, or other noncreature spell before combat.
- **Board development:** turn that spell into a Wall and let token engines create additional bodies.
- **Conversion:** use protection, high-toughness payoffs, token scaling, and attack pressure to turn a defensive board into a win.

That changes how cards should be evaluated. A cheap answer such as **An Offer You Can’t Refuse** is more valuable here than it would be in a normal midrange deck because it protects the engine, triggers Invisible Woman, and leaves mana available for the commander’s combat ability. A large creature that does none of those jobs may be powerful but still be a poor draw.

The first play-pattern rule is straightforward: **try to cast a noncreature spell before combat whenever it is safe to do so.** Do not burn the only spell in hand just to create a token if holding it protects the commander or stops a must-answer permanent. The goal is not to trigger Invisible Woman at any cost; it is to create a repeatable loop where your normal interaction also develops your board.

## Upgrade path one: make the commander reliable

The first wave should improve consistency before adding expensive token doublers. Start with cards that are useful when the battlefield is empty and still advance the commander plan when the board is established.

### First additions

- **Swords to Plowshares** gives the deck one-mana exile removal.
- **Counterspell** protects Invisible Woman, a token engine, or a decisive spell.
- **Beast Within** answers any permanent type.
- **Nature’s Lore** increases early fixing without adding another clunky mana rock.
- **An Offer You Can’t Refuse** is a cheap instant-speed trigger and protection spell.
- **Heroic Intervention** protects the board that the deck spends several turns building.
- **Swiftfoot Boots** gives Invisible Woman protection and haste.
- **Propaganda** buys time against creature-heavy tables.
- **Restorative Technique** provides inexpensive recovery for a destroyed engine.

This package is intentionally modest. It creates more hands that can ramp, cast the commander, and still hold up a spell for the next combat. It also keeps the deck from becoming dependent on drawing a specific token payoff.

## Upgrade path two: turn one spell into several bodies

Once the spell-and-protection floor is stable, add engines that multiply each noncreature spell.

**Shark Typhoon** is the standout upgrade. It can be cycled as an instant to trigger the commander, or it can remain on the battlefield and turn later noncreature spells into flying Sharks. That second mode is especially important because it gives the deck an evasive route to victory rather than asking Walls to do every job.

**Monastery Mentor, Third Path Iconoclast,** and **Young Pyromancer** are the budget-friendly spell-to-creature package. They make the deck’s ordinary interaction produce a board. **Storm-Kiln Artist** adds Treasures instead, which is valuable because the Fantastic Four’s activated abilities ask for colored mana and the deck often wants to cast more than one spell in a turn.

For card advantage, **Caretaker’s Talent, Idol of Oblivion,** and **Archmage Emeritus** keep the engine from running out of gas. Idol of Oblivion is particularly appropriate when the deck is producing tokens every turn; Archmage Emeritus is better when the build contains a heavier instant-and-sorcery package.

## Upgrade path three: make the Walls lethal

Invisible Woman’s Walls are not supposed to remain harmless forever. The cleanest conversion package is:

- **High Alert** — lets high-toughness creatures attack using toughness.
- **Assault Formation** — a second high-toughness payoff for a dedicated Wall version.
- **Axebane Guardian** — turns a cluster of Walls into a real mana engine.
- **Arcades, the Strategist** — a strong alternate commander and a useful 99-card Wall payoff.
- **Impact Tremors** — gives every new token an immediate damage role.

High Alert is the most important purchase in this package because it changes the purpose of the Wall tokens without requiring a large board. Impact Tremors is the best backup plan: even when the table makes combat difficult, repeated token creation still moves opponents toward a lethal range.

Do not add every Wall card at once. A token/spellslinger build wants enough creatures to defend itself, but it should not become so creature-heavy that it loses the cheap noncreature spells that turn Invisible Woman on.

## Upgrade path four: multiply the board and the mana

Token doublers are powerful only when the deck has a reliable token engine. Buy them after Shark Typhoon, a spell-to-creature payoff, and a card-draw engine are already working.

- **Parallel Lives** is the cleanest permanent token multiplier, but it is the largest early expense.
- **Adrix and Nev, Twincasters** provides a second multiplier and a creature body.
- **Cryptolith Rite** converts a wide token board into the colored mana needed for a major spell chain or multiple Fantastic Four activations.
- **Second Harvest** is the budget-friendly burst option when a permanent doubler is outside the budget.

The ideal sequence is not “cast a token doubler and hope.” It is “establish a token engine, cast the doubler, then use a cheap spell to trigger Invisible Woman and multiply the entire turn’s output.”

## Upgrade path five: protect the investment

A Wall/token deck is vulnerable to a single sweeper because its board is also its card advantage, mana, and win condition. Protection should be layered:

- Keep **Clever Concealment** from the precon.
- Add **Heroic Intervention** as the first broad protection upgrade.
- Use **Swiftfoot Boots** to protect the commander.
- Add cheap stack interaction such as **Counterspell** and **An Offer You Can’t Refuse**.
- Consider **Rootborn Defenses** when the deck has a wide token board.
- Treat **Fierce Guardianship** and **Deflecting Swat** as premium, cross-deck purchases rather than required upgrades.

The premium cards are excellent, but they are not where this deck gets its first major improvement. A $1–$3 spell that triggers Invisible Woman and answers a threat is often a better first purchase than a luxury free counterspell.

## A practical budget build

### Around $25: consistency and identity

Start with **Swords to Plowshares, Counterspell, Beast Within, Nature’s Lore, An Offer You Can’t Refuse, Tamiyo’s Safekeeping, Third Path Iconoclast, Young Pyromancer, High Alert, Impact Tremors, Idol of Oblivion,** and **Rootborn Defenses**.

This version interacts cheaply, creates more bodies, draws from its token plan, and turns high toughness into real combat pressure.

### Around $50: the deck starts to feel complete

Add **Shark Typhoon, Storm-Kiln Artist, Archmage Emeritus, Swiftfoot Boots, Propaganda, Caretaker’s Talent, Strionic Resonator,** and **Murmuring Mystic**.

Strionic Resonator is a particularly nice Invisible Woman upgrade because it provides a budget way to copy a triggered ability. It does not replace every function of Lithoform Engine, but it lets the deck reproduce an important commander trigger without paying premium prices.

### Around $100 and beyond: commitment upgrades

Add **Cryptolith Rite, Parallel Lives, Adrix and Nev, Twincasters, Improvisation Capstone, Echocasting Symposium,** and **Germination Practicum**. Only then consider **Doubling Season, Fierce Guardianship, Deflecting Swat, Rhystic Study,** or **Smothering Tithe**.

Those premium cards are better purchases when they can move between several decks in the collection. The full ManaBox export should be imported first so the tracker can identify cards already owned or sitting in other decks.

## What to cut from the stock list

The best cuts are not necessarily the weakest cards in isolation. They are the cards that do the least for Invisible Woman’s specific plan.

The first candidates to test are **Galactus, Devourer of Worlds, Silver Surfer, Galactus’s Herald, Mind’s Dilation, Genesis Ultimatum, Annie Joins Up, Mirage Mirror, Path of Discovery,** and **Taunt from the Rampart**. These cards are not unplayable, but they are slower, more situational, or less connected to creating and exploiting the Wall/token board.

Do not cut every sweeper. Keep enough reset effects to recover when an opposing deck develops faster. The upgrade goal is not to remove the precon’s ability to answer a board; it is to ensure that your own board is the one that benefits most from the next turn.

## Invisible Woman at the table

A good opening hand contains three lands or two lands plus ramp, one cheap noncreature spell, and either protection or a token engine. A hand full of six-mana creatures is not a keep simply because the deck has four colors.

Fix blue and green early when possible. Blue supports the cheap interaction and card flow; green supports the ramp and Wall-based mana plan. White and red become more important as the deck starts using its removal and Fantastic Four combat abilities.

Do not cast Invisible Woman automatically on turn four. If the table is not pressuring you, it can be better to establish an engine first or wait until you can cast her with protection. She is strongest when a spell is ready to trigger her and the resulting combat step is worth protecting.

## Final verdict

The best Invisible Woman upgrade is not the most expensive version. It is the version where every part of the deck does at least two jobs: interaction triggers the commander, tokens draw cards, Walls make mana, and protection also advances the board.

Start with cheap spells and reliable token engines. Add High Alert and Impact Tremors to create multiple ways to win. Then decide whether the deck wants permanent token multiplication or premium protection. If the deck consistently creates a board and survives the first sweeper, the expensive upgrades will feel like finishers rather than repairs.

For the current collection project, the next operational step is to import the full ManaBox export. That will allow the tracker to separate **Already Owned**, **Conditional Transfer**, and **Buy** recommendations before any shopping list becomes final.

## Sources and methodology

- [EDHREC — The Fantastic Four / Invisible Woman upgrade page](https://edhrec.com/precons/the-fantastic-four/invisible-woman)
- [Wizards of the Coast — Marvel Super Heroes Commander decklists](https://magic.wizards.com/en/news/announcements/marvel-super-heroes-commander-decklists)
- [Card Kingdom — Marvel Super Heroes Fantastic Four Commander upgrade guide](https://blog.cardkingdom.com/marvel-super-heroes-fantastic-four-commander-deck-upgrade-guide/)
- [Scryfall API documentation](https://scryfall.com/docs/api)
